resume its consideration of sub-item B of agenda item 2, thematic review, to hold an interactive panel discussion on the theme Small Island Developing States: Strategies for SDG Success. There is no doubt that small island developing states remain a special case for sustainable development. We are already one year into the implementation of the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for Small Island Developing States. Recently, two international conferences were held, namely the Third United Nations Conference to support the implementation of Sustainable Development Goal 14, conserve and sustainably use the ocean, seas, and marine resources for sustainable development, as well as the 4th International Conference on Financing for Development. They both have the potential to unblock to unlock much-needed development finance at scale and to establish effective partnerships that mobilize the necessary means of implementation to ensure tangible results for Small Island Developing States. Today's discussion will examine early efforts to support the effective implementation of the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for Small Island Developing States. I am now pleased to welcome our panelists. Her Excellency Ilana Said, Permanent Representative of Palau to the United Nations and Chair of the Alliance of Small Small Island States. Mr. Navid Hanif, Assistant Secretary-General for Economic Development in the Department of Economic and Social Affairs, and Mr. Sergio Fernández de Córdoba, Executive Chairman of the Public Foundation. I also welcome our lead discussant, Ms. Ruth Julie Kissam from Advancing PNG Women Leaders Network. I am also pleased to welcome the moderator, Mr. Matthew Bishop, Co-Director of the Resilient and Sustainable Islands Initiative. I now hand the floor over to the moderator to begin the discussion.

Good afternoon, everybody. Thank you for joining us. We have a panel discussion now to talk about some of the things that SIDS can be doing in order to try and catch up with the SDG process. And I've got a series of questions to pose to the panel, beginning with a general question which I will throw out to, to all of them. There's 3 parts to this question. The first one is, what do you see as the core priority areas for action that could facilitate that meaningful catch-up and progress? The second part is how can the outcomes of related processes like FFD4, UNOC 3, and the upcoming WSSD2 be strategically harnessed to mobilize the support that SIDS urgently need? And then the final part is how can the international partnerships that SIDS rely on for progress be expanded or deepened? So I'll hand over and give the floor to Ambassador Syed to kick us off.

Thank you very much, Mr. Moderator. And first, let me express my sincere appreciation to you and to the organizers of the SIDS segment in presenting a clear picture of where SIDS find themselves in the wider global geopolitical and economic landscape. Certainly, the regression of action and commitments, whether that's in financing and ODA, in climate change, in trade, or multilateralism generally, SIDS are in, quite honestly, a very precarious position and are at great risk of falling behind. On that note, I must emphasize that as chair of AOSIS, our core priority areas as SIDS lie in unlocking the means of implementation, particularly financing, technology, and capacity building, and that's needed for us to build resilience and foster economic growth. However, to do this, it requires deliberate actions both at the national and international levels. Three areas that require require urgent action. First, we need the system and the international community to fully recognize the special circumstances of SIDS, which gives rise to us being a special case for sustainable development. This requires the UN system, the international financial institutions, and other international bodies to see and address the specific needs of SIDS through tailored programmatic support and policies. Second, through this recognition, we need to expand the fiscal space available to SIDS by unlocking access to concessional and grant-based financing, and eligibility must go beyond GDP per capita. The Multidimensional Vulnerability Index, otherwise known as the MDI, has now been endorsed by the UN General Assembly, and it must be integrated into development and financing decisions, especially concessional finance, as well as graduation policies for SIDS. Third, we need to strengthen data and institutional capacity to deliver on the commitments in the ABAS. This means support for tools and mechanisms aimed at building SIDS capacities, including the SIDS Center for Excellence, the SIDS Global Data Hub, and the Debt Sustainability Support Service, DSSS. Without adequate long-term capacity building, our collective efforts will not deliver on our objectives. Thank you, Mr. Moderator.
Wonderful. Thank you. We'll move over now to Mr. Dikodova. Sergio?

Thank you, Matthew. Well, we believe that when you start to look at the small island development states and what's been happening, we need to build infrastructure, an infrastructure that you can't see. Which is data. We need the technologies, we need the capacity building, and without real-time geospatial sovereign data and without the ability to actually implement these tools, this is why we need the SIDS Global Data Hub and the Center of Excellence, because we need a mechanism by which to bring stakeholders together. No longer can we look at a framework and actually have 100 people doing the same exact thing. We need to work together, we need to bring public and private together, we need to bring the foundations, we need to bring the technologies, And we must move differently than we have. Traditional aid won't cut it. We need solutions that are actually going to bring technologies, that are going to bring solutions, and are going to help us actually fulfill the outcomes of FFD4, UNOC 3, and a lot of these platforms and frameworks that have actually— are showing us the path, but now we need to actually make— take action and bring together execution.
Wonderful, thanks. And I'll now go over to Assistant Secretary General Hanif.

Thank you, Mr. Moderator. You have asked a fairly big question, so I will need a little bit of time because a lot has happened. And I also want to commend the President and the Bureau of the Council to dedicate 3 hours for such conversation at the High-Level Political Forum. They need this attention. So the policy objectives for SIDS, first and foremost, we need to— and this requires domestic and international action— is to shockproof these vulnerable countries. That should be our first priority, and that requires domestic policies, domestic planning that is designed to promote self-sustaining investments in human capital, in institutions, in attracting foreign investment. And there I find the tool of Integrated National Financing Framework, sustainable development strategies, which should be multi-sectoral and designed in such a fashion that they take into account specific needs of SIDS at the same time recognize their diversity. On the international side, and I will bring in the CVA commitments, four key provisions which are critical for SIDS to pursue, but on the international side the challenge for SIDS we have witnessed repeatedly is managing their external debt, unsustainable debt servicing burden,, and we need to pursue proposals on debt swaps and other measures to reduce this burden and create fiscal space and also increase their tax-to-GDP ratio. The Suiya commitment, I think, is an important milestone for SIDS. This is the first FFD document which has recognized the need to go beyond GDP, look at their vulnerabilities which are not just driven by income criteria, and I think this should become a norm in all decisions which allocate concessional finance. Then there is a commitment to improve development cooperation, and that means aid effectiveness and better impact on all concessional finance. Then, appeal to IFIs and MDBs to adopt Multidimensional Vulnerability Index as a complementary tool to guide their decisions. This is the third breakthrough in the Sevilla Commitment for SIDS. And lastly, the— and Ambassador mentioned— Debt Sustainability Support Service. The Sevilla Commitment had asked for acceleration in implementing the services. These four areas have come out of the severe commitment. And from the oceans conference, I want to highlight one point which is actually critical for this economic transformation, and that is growth models that are based on the ocean sector. So your dependence on external linkages is relatively reduced. It can't be totally eliminated. Thank you, Mr. Malfoy.

Thank you very much, Assistant Secretary General. I'm now going to target a question to each of the panelists that's a bit more focused in terms of their own remits, beginning again with Ambassador Said. So you've inherited the AOSIS chair at a time when the remit facing the organization is expanding.— but global financial resources are diminishing at the same time, and that's quite a tough picture to cope with. How do you see AOSIS coping with this dilemma? How can you use AOSIS' strengths to support and leverage the resources needed to scale up the implementation of the SDGs?

Thank you very much, Mr. Moderator. SIDS certainly have— we've never been passive actors. One of the things that I kind of think about collectively is the SIDS comprise 20% of the UN vote. It's 39 members. It's quite a large bloc, and we are— our voices are very important in the areas of climate, the areas of ocean and sustainable development. But I think we are— we finally kind of reached a moment where we are strongly advocating for ourselves. And I think even though some may say the pie is shrinking, I think AOCSIS has a very strong position to take up a larger share of the pie that it should have gotten in the first place. So I think I would say that, that, that, that's something that we are— we collectively are stewards of 30% of the world's oceans. That's a big responsibility, but we need the resources to be able to mobilize some of the commitments and some of the priorities that we have as ocean countries. So through the ABAS, we have a unified and visionary 10-year plan And it's not just a declaration, it's an investment framework. And we're currently working on M&E, monitoring and evaluation framework, to make sure that some of the goals that we've set forth in the Abassah are actually met. The operationalization of the SIDS Center of Excellence is critical to making this happen. And we're also reaching out to non-traditional partners. We're looking at innovative financing mechanisms to to fill gaps and creatively reach our pressing challenges. We are looking to things like South-South cooperation, which are even more important with traditional donors kind of diminishing their ODA. And we're also looking to the private sector. I think our colleague here mentioned the importance of data, and we're looking to technology companies to come and really help us strengthen some of the— that critical infrastructure, but also ways that we can work together. So whether it's through the UN system, the MDBs and IFIs, or like-minded partners, I think programmatic partnerships is going to be crucial to ensuring the successful implementation of ABAS. We understand the climate we're in, but we also understand that we need to kind of take control of our own destinies, and we hope that the next 10 years will be transformational for us. Thank you.

Wonderful. So the comment about non-traditional or innovative sources of finance, I think, kind of comes into the question I'm about to ask Sergio. So the Public Foundation was instrumental in supporting Antigua and Barbuda and SIDS more generally in laying the groundwork for establishing the SIDS Center of Excellence, and in particular the Global Data Hub. Can you update us a bit on what's happening with the Data Hub and what the international community can expect to see moving forward as it becomes operationalized? What also, in your, in your view, also what are the major challenges for SIDS with respect to strengthening the national data systems that you kind of mentioned earlier? What investments are needed? And is the Global Data Hub intended to bridge these gaps and challenges? And if so, how? I realize there's a lot there, Sergio.

Thank you, Mr. Moderator. At its core, the SIDS Global Data Hub represents a transformative shift towards sovereign data ownership, institutional capacity, and regional interoperability, which is very important for the SIDS. The ambition is clear: to ensure that every Small Island Development State can access secure, real-time, and policy-relevant data to inform national strategies, track SDG implementations, and unlock new opportunities across sectors—from ocean governance, as we heard about, UNOC 3, to sustainable tourism, trade, and environmental resilience. We introduced a Global Data Hub prototype at the SIDS IV, refined it through the engagement at UNGA COP 29 and regional workshops across the Caribbean, Caribbean, and the Pacific. And in 2025, we're scaling it to establish it in 10 fully interoperable country hubs. These will serve as national anchor points feeding into the global data hub and global hubs, creating an integrated sovereign data system that reflects the realities and priorities of SIDS. The importance of data is really to have real-time information, but the challenges still remain. The 3 most pressing barriers are limited digital infrastructure and broadband access, a shortage of long-term technical data professionals within the government institution, and fragmented data ecosystems where valuable information remains inaccessible. So to bridge these gaps, the Data Hub is designed to complement national systems, not replacement— not replace them at all. It provides shared software and secured cloud infrastructure. Standardized governance models that keeps data at a source while making it visible and actionable, ongoing capacity building and technical support through the Center of Excellence. This is not simply a digital tool. It is a multilateral infrastructure for resilience co-created with the governments themselves, supported with private sector technology and innovation, and designed to strengthen institutional sovereignty over time. As we move forward, sustained investment will be critical, as mentioned earlier. We need all the stakeholders. Everyone must be part of the conversation. When we look at, especially in national data officer roles, capacity building— again, was mentioned earlier— capacity building is key in these communities and being able to not only transfer technology but transfer intelligence so that folks actually can be the, the leaders that we need them to be within the ministries. The public cloud and hybrid systems that support real-time analytics that isn't controlled by private sector, but rather controlled at the sovereign national level. Small catalytic grants that help enable ministries to activate and share key datasets. Being that a lot of organizations, as I mentioned earlier, we have hundreds of groups that are doing a lot for the SIDS, but nobody is coming together. And a lot of the vision that has been put together with the ABES is to really in the Center of Excellence is to bring everybody together so that we're not creating in parallels, but rather creating together. In short, the SIDS Data— Global Data Hub is more than a platform. It is a foundation for evidence-based governance, cross-regional solidarity, and economic transfer— transformation through data, which is key. A lot of what we talk about is economic development through data. Thank you, Miss Moderator.

Wonderful, thank you very, very much. And then the final focus question is for Assistant Secretary-General Hanif. Can you share some of your reflections on these issues from the UN side, given that SIDS all face similar challenges, as you said just now, but have their particular kinds of distinctive characteristics? What work is DESA doing to support their special case in terms of achieving the SDGs? How are you grappling with implementing these different processes on different time horizons?, and what is happening within the UN system to push forward initiatives like MVI implementation or the Debt Sustainability Support Service? What other mechanisms do we need, and are there other opportunities that you're excited about? Again, another big question there.

Thank you so much, Mr. Moderator. Before I respond to this question, I just want to respond to Sergio's observation on data collection, tabulation, deploying it for policymaking. These are challenges which are widely shared among SIDS, but there are solutions available that the UN system is advancing from— through initiatives like Data Now, urgency of using data in evidence-based policymaking. So that priority is high for the UN system. And I also want to emphasize DESA is always trying to bring the system together to avoid duplication, overlap, unnecessary competition. So that effort is ongoing and the Department of Economic and Social Affairs has done that since the adoption of the first SIDS Programme of Action. Now, Mr. Moderator, there are 3 questions you have asked me in one breath. First is diversity and distinction. So what— in our department, there are four striking shared structural challenges for SIDS which we have to keep in mind supporting any small island developing states. First and foremost is the geographic isolation. Second is narrow economic base. Third is climate and disaster risks, and fourthly, debt sustainability and fiscal space. Almost all SIDS share these structural challenges, so we have to keep those in mind while responding to SIDS, be it in the Pacific, in the Caribbean, or Indian Ocean. So with those in mind, what we are trying to do is have a modular approach, develop modules which also look at the specific needs tailored to their national and regional tracks. For instance, when we talk of digital transformation, data and statistics, financing, science and technology, innovation and partnerships, we customize these interventions depending on specific states' needs. This we have done particularly in digital transformation Our capacity building work, which usually goes through country teams, is customized for countries' needs depending on their human resource capacity, their digital infrastructure, and their needs. So this is how we are in designing our interventions. Then we also are promoting learning from peer learning among SIDS, and that's also a program which built around STI efforts through peer learning. Then using regional grouping strategically so that we at least can focus at the regional level. For instance, tax policy is an area where regional approaches can work. So let me say what we are trying to do is knowledge exchange, regional cooperation, sub-regional collaboration, especially when they are developing projects for investment, and that's what our advice has been to SIDS at the SEG Investment Fair: look for scale through sub-regional cooperation. Now, the second part of your question is what is happening to the UN processes on MVI. So there is an assessment going on of the best UN institutions to host the UN Secretariat and identification of the MVI panel. So UN system is taking these actions and continued advocacy for the use of MDI and IFRs and MDBs. And UN system is pilot testing the MDI and examining the feasibility of mainstreaming the tool. Opportunities at the World Summit on Social Development. I think one— two areas stand out in the outcome document. One is Social protection, how do you— first, every country should legislate it, and then how should you finance social protection? Second is social inclusion, and what are the economic policies that should be designed to promote social inclusion in societies, or for all groups, vulnerable and otherwise? So on the first, we are working with ILO in coming up with policy tools which will help countries both in having budgetary allocations for social protection, but also in times of crisis and shocks, some access to some financial instruments that they can tap into immediately to protect their citizens from those shocks and their impact. So these are some of the ideas which we are going to advance. Through the World Summit on Social Development in Doha, and we are keen that SIDS should get special attention at the social summit. Thank you.

Fantastic, thank you. Before coming to the final question, I'd like to reflect just a little bit on some of the conversation that we've just heard, and it seems to me, in tying together some of the different things that you've all said, the key kind of challenge going forward for SIDS is about unlocking what Ambassador Syed described as the means of implementation, right? So we need to expand fiscal space in a context where fiscal space is constrained, where many SIDS are struggling with heavy debt burdens, as we all know. We need to access new and innovative sources of private and philanthropic finance while building new infrastructures to harness technology and data. That seems to me the kind of key practical challenge going forward. I just wonder if each of you would mind just talking a little bit more about your kind of individual vision for that. What does that actually look like in practice for you, and how does that get rolled out to SIDS as a whole? We'll start with Ambassador Saeed again.

Thank you very much. It's a very important question. I think there can't be sustainable development without sustainable access to finance, and we've always advocated as EOSIS that the special circumstances of SIDS and the unique vulnerabilities that we have need to shape the policies that allow us to access cheap, affordable, and predictable finance. So maybe just to paint a picture of why SIDS are different from some of the other larger developing countries. If you are a large country and you are on a— you get to a middle or high income level, you have other sources where you can access finance, whether that's through the capital markets, that's through foreign direct investment. There are other venues where you can, you can generate finance so that your growth is continued. That's very challenging for SIDS because a lot of investment banks view SIDS as too small, so they won't actually take you into the capital markets. And the economies of scale for most, for a lot of SIDS, remain challenging for a lot of the foreign direct investment partners. So that's why we've always advocated that looking at metrics beyond GDP per capita is important. So I think a big success for SIDS would be for the MDBs and IFIs to incorporate things like the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index into the, the programmatic approach in which we can access concessional and grant finance. I think of just another very specific example is my own country of Palau. We have graduated. We then meet this hurdle where, when we go to the big MDBs, the cost of finance is prohibitively high. And so we are faced with then typhoons where we have a large part of our economy swept away. We have to go and get loans. And so we get into this kind of negative debt cycle. And then we have to ungraduate. So we actually ungraduated because of COVID and we are doing okay now, and we're about to graduate again. But we are kind of facing this— it's kind of like a car engine that won't quite start properly. So we need the financial system to recognize that SIDS are different so that the programs are actually tailored to our specific needs so we can reach this kind of state of what economists call escape velocity, so that you can continue to grow. So I think that's— if we were able to get accessible, affordable finance, we can invest in resilient infrastructure so that the increasing storms don't impact us quite as well. We can recover from climate shocks, and then we can also build and recover for long-term sustainability. Thank you.

I think that's right. That cost of capital question is crucial, isn't it? When we think that, you know, 100% debt burden is a lot for any country, but the financing of that for a much larger, wealthier country, even in a high interest rate environment, can still be very low at 3 or 4% a year. For Sid's country, that can be 30%, 50% of government revenues. I mean, this is a staggering difference. So even when you look at headline debt burdens, they also don't really tell the whole story. Sergio, I'll hand over to you on that question.

Thank you, Mr. Moderator. When I think about, you know, the work, though, especially what we're doing across data systems, financing platforms, and public-private collaboration, which I think is key in this conversation, we see the Future of ABIS as not just as a policy document, but as an operational blueprint for sovereign resilience led through center of excellence and understanding the data. And when we look at the approach, we look at it from 3 strategic pillars that are directly advancing the ABES priorities. Number 1 is institutionalizing data sovereignty towards a beyond GDP framework, right? As we heard Ambassador speak about the beyond GDP, it's not just an element that will help the countries drive forward, but also the community and the people in each of the countries. At the heart of ABES is a call for control over data. Not just as a tool for reporting, but as a foundation of power, planning, and prosperity for their communities and their economies. Number 2 is we look at designing nature-positive economic systems. Right? The Abas speaks about how clearly the value of natural capital— and also we look at Beyond GDP, we look at nature as a producer, as a GDP, through platforms like the Development Bank for Resilient Prosperity, NatureBank, and work around real-world natural assets. We could help move the SIDS forwards from climate vulnerability to climate opportunity and look at nature as an opportunity to build resilience and economic development by valuing ecosystems and infrastructure, pricing resilience into national planning, and unlocking blended capital scale. Again, as the Ambassador said, having— bringing in new capital sources that understand where the future is going. And number 3, operationalizing global partnerships. Right? In the ABIS, it calls for revitalized international cooperation, right? So, not just multilaterals, but also looking at family offices, looking at foundations, new institutions that are focused on where the future is going, institutional partnerships supporting the UN initiatives, as, you know, as was mentioned as well with the work that DESA is doing, and regional bodies and governments, and how public-private coalitions are not just symbolic, but are being brought in as an opportunity to help bring in and drive capital, and building bridges between government sovereign needs, private capital, foundations, and humanity. In short, I think that there is an incredible future here as long as we follow the roadmap and the blueprint that we've all set out to implement.
Brilliant. Thanks, Sergio. I'll hand over to Assistant Secretary General Hanif.

Thank you so much. I cannot overemphasize the role of public finance in development. Public finance which is predictable, accessible, reliable, concessional. And I also want to emphasize domestic public finance is equally important. Governments cannot walk away from their responsibility. On development, on fighting climate action. So to do— what do we need? Climate action, anyone— I hope no one believes private sector can alone fight it or reverse it. That is, I think, a travesty for humanity to think without public finance we can fight climate action. And Czar at the forefront of climate impact. So first and foremost, public finance has to be made available to SIDS on concessional terms. How? CVA has 3 actions very clearly: triple the MDB capital base, give them the capacity to lend, and give special preferential treatment to SIDS from that stream. Second, there is a agreement in the Sevilla Commitment, new playbook for SDRs. We know there are challenges in creating more liquidity, but special drawing rights should be considered as another source of expanding public finance. I am not underestimating the technical difficulties, but it is in the Sevilla Commitment. Third, and that's also repeatedly mentioned by SIDS and many other open facilities when they're hit by a shock. RST is a welcome development after COVID. IMF has done it, but more facilities when cities are hit by shocks, public finance should be immediately available. They don't have to wait to go through long processes. So we have to be bold, innovative in thinking. Second stream which we have learned since Adisa Baba Private money will not move on its own to these destinations. You need to deploy public money through guarantees and other means to move money where it is badly needed. So that pool of money should be created, and that's nothing unusual. Is public money going to the moon, developing vaccines? It was always the public money that led and private money followed. So that is second level of action on means of implementation—deploy public money domestically and internationally to move private investment where it is needed. Third, and I want to welcome—DAC is undertaking a review in Paris to revisit their ODA practices, and I understand they have this consideration, how can they look beyond income and look at vulnerabilities. It's a welcome initiative. By DAC. So ODA allocation criteria may be revisited and adjusted to allocate it to SIDS, because there are countries who are not by choice— were dependent on ODA, they need it. And if criteria are revisited, their vulnerabilities will become a factor to have them better flows. And lastly, on debt management, I really want to encourage SIDS, there are two avenues open at the United Nations. One is join Debtors Club or Debtors Forum. There's agreement now, so we are Debtors Club that will be launched. SIDS should be actively engaged to come together as debtors and see how can you advance peer learning and solution finding. Secondly, there will be a dialogue at the United Nations to look at the debt architecture. You should be active participants. In shaping that dialogue and see it works for you. Thank you, Mr. Mukherjee.

Wonderful. This has been an exceptionally enriching conversation. I'm going to ask each of the panellists to look forward now in the final question. What for you is the one big success that you would like to see SIDS achieve in terms of sustainable development by 2030, and how would that prepare the ground for whatever follows the SDGs?, I presume, from 2030 onwards, and then of course SIDS V, which will be already upon us just a few years after that. Begin with Ambassador Syed.

Thank you, Mr. Moderator. I think maybe just going back to my last response is, if we can get accessible sustainable finance for SIDS right, I think that would go a long way in unlocking a lot of the sustainable development challenges. Also getting climate finance right. It's access to finance both for development and also for climate as well, as well as ocean finances. As I had mentioned in one of my earlier statements that we are ocean countries, SDG 14 is one of the least funded SDGs. As a result, the finance available for SIDS countries for ocean development is also quite limited. If we're able to get that right, I think we can see that SIDS 5— the SIDS development profile will look vastly different. Thank you.
Wonderful. Thank you. Sergio.

Thank you, Matthew. By 2030, we believe the greatest success can be— can help collectively with the small island development states achieve the establishment of resilient, data-driven, and nature-powered economic systems. Where natural capital is recognized as national wealth and digital infrastructure enables sovereign decisions in real time, like the rest of the world operates. This means going beyond survival. It means positioning the SIDS as a global leader in sustainable development, where economies are not only climate smart but structurally designed to align ecological integrity with financial stability and long-term prosperity. They call them the least developed, but are they least developed or are they the wealthiest? If achieved, this is not only prepares the SIDS for the post-SDG era, but it sets the tone for it. Because what comes after 2030 will demand new models, ones rooted on resilience, equity, and regeneration. And no group is better positioned to lead this paradigm shift than the Small Island Development States, the custodian of the world's oceans, biodiversity, and frontline innovation. As we look on to— which is a great question— SIDS V, this vision offers more than a roadmap. It offers a legacy, one where island nations are no longer viewed through the lens of vulnerability, vulnerability, but also through the lens of leadership, through the lens of sustainability, as architects of the next generation of global development frameworks. How it should be done. But this will require serious international commitment to finance the systems that value ecosystems, to embed data capacities at the core of public institutions, and to scale partnerships and move beyond pledges into performance. SIDS don't need incremental change. They need bold, integrated investments across nature, data, and innovation that turns their greatest challenges into the world's most scalable solutions. This is the kind of success we should all be working towards by 2030 and beyond, not just for SIDS V, but for the SIDS as a whole and for the global system that they're helping to redefine.
Wonderful, thank you. And finally, Assistant Secretary-General Hani.
You ask me one big thing. Diversified and shock resilient economies. That's it. Thank you.
Wonderful. So at this point, we're going to invite Ms. Ruth Julie Kissam from the Advancing PNG Women Leaders Network, who is going to act as our discussant. Ruth.

I am a tribal woman leader from Papua New Guinea, a nation of immense biodiversity, home to the world's third-largest intact tropical rainforest and vibrant indigenous cultures. Yet we stand at a critical crossroad in the global climate crisis. As a small island developing state, we face existential threats from rising sea and extreme weather. Yet we are also one of the world's last lines of defense against catastrophic climate change. Today, I underscore why PNG and SIDS and other SIDS are a special case in climate negotiation and why the international community must act with urgency and equity to support our nation and other SIDS like us. PNG's forests span 70% of the landmass. It is a global carbon sink under threat. These forests store billions of tons of carbon, host 7% of the world's biodiversity, sustains the livelihoods and cultural survival of millions of indigenous people who have stewarded these lands for millennia. Yet despite our minimal contribution to global emissions, PNG's forests are under siege from illegal logging, unsustainable agriculture, and resource extraction. If lost, the released carbon would undo decades of global climate progress. Papua New Guinea is the classic paradox of a low emitter facing high climate risks. Unlike our major polluters, PNG did not create this crisis, yet like many other seeds, we bear its heaviest burdens. This is a profound injustice. A call for climate justice and urgent support. PNG cannot protect its forests and adapt to climate change without immediate scaled-up support under the principles of climate justice in the Paris Agreement. We demand increased climate finance, recognition of Indigenous stewardship, debt-for-nature swap and carbon markets, technology and capacity transfer. We are not just another vulnerable seed. We are a global climate lifeline. Our forests are a natural solution the world cannot afford to lose, but without fair partnership, we risk becoming another victim of climate colonialism. Papua New Guinea's future depends on balance between progress and preservation, between global demands and local rights. Let us build partnership that honors this balance. In conclusion, the world needs PNG's forest and PNG needs the world's support. Papua New Guinea is not just another We did not start the fire, but our forests helped put it out. It is time the world recognizes our value, not just as victims, but as vital partners in the fight for our shared future. In the words of my ancestors, "We did not inherit the land from our parents. We borrow it from our children." Let our partnership reflect this wisdom.

Thank you very much, Ruth. And at this point, that wraps up the panel conversation, and I pass back to the chair. I very much thank the panelists for the thoughts that they have shared. I thank the moderator, and I also thank our lead discussant. I now would like to ask you to give us a warm round of applause to thank the panelists. We will now begin the interactive discussion. Gracias, Senhora Presidente. Thank you very much, Madam President. I have the honor to deliver the message by His Excellency His Excellency Honourable José Ulisses Correia e Silva, Prime Minister of the Republic of Cabo Verde. Madam President, Excellency, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen. It is a great honour to join you today at this critical juncture as we gather under the theme of Advancing Sustainable, Inclusive Science and Evidence-Based Solutions for the 2030 Agenda. I bring you warm greetings from Cabo Verde, a proud small island developing state that just celebrated its 50th anniversary of independence a couple of days ago, and the nation steadfastly committed to the SDGs. This high-level political forum especially timely, coming one year after the Fourth International Conference of SIDS and the adoption of the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS, and in the wake of the Third UN Conference for— sorry, the Third UN Ocean Conference and the Fourth UN Conference on Financing for Development, realized last June and at the beginning of this month. Their outcome documents, the ABAS, NIS Declaration, and the Compromiso de Sevilla, provide us with bold blueprint for action grounded in the realities of our islands and aligned with the broader aspirations of the Pact for the Future. The success of ABAS will depend on our ability to align national strategies with its core pillars: resilience, inclusion, and innovation. In Cabo Verde, we are integrating the ABAS commitments into our national development plan with a focus on sustainable ocean governance, digital transformation, and blue and green economy pathways. But implementation cannot be business as usual. It requires a whole-of-society approach, engaging youth, civil society, the private sector, and traditional knowledge holders. For ABAS to succeed, ownership at the national and community level is essential, and SIDS must be supported to build the institutional and technical capacity to lead this process. Despite our vulnerabilities, SIDS are also laboratories of innovation. In Cabo Verde, we are piloting digital health solutions to extend care to the remote islands, investing in desalination powered by renewables, and advancing climate-smart agriculture to boost food security. SIDS are not just recipients of innovation, but also creators and exporters of context-specific solutions, from, from early warning systems to sustainable fisheries management. What we need now is the global recognition and scaling up of these homegrown innovations through inclusive technology transfer and impact partnerships. No SIDS can walk the path alone. Regional cooperation through mechanisms like ICE-SIDS coordination, UN regional commissions, and South-South cooperation are essential to pool expertise and amplify our voices. That's why last May, Cabo Verde organized and hosted an ICE-SIDS high-level meeting in Praia. During the meeting, we established a coordination mechanism chaired by Cabo Verde during its inaugural mandate, and which will help us to better coordinate among ourselves and scale up projects for common presentation and/or development. But we must go farther, and therefore the international community must watch its commitments with predictable long-term support and become a catalyst for transformative, accountable partnership that places it at the center, not the periphery, of global cooperation. Excellencies, friends, achieving the SDGs requires that finance flows match ambition. Yet many SIDS remain trapped in structural debt burden and face barriers to concessional financing due to outdated income classifications. We must urgently operationalize the MVI to ensure that access to finance reflects the real lived vulnerabilities of our countries. At the same time, innovative mechanisms such as Blue Bonds, Debt-for-Nature swaps, and blended finance models must be mainstreamed and scaled. Cap Verde is currently working on a climate finance strategy aimed at leveraging public and private capital for resilience building. But no SIDS should have to navigate this alone. International financial institutions and development partners must support capacity development and risk-sharing instruments to unlock capital at scale. We, the SIDS, are the sentinels of the world's oceans and the conscience of our collective ambition. 99% of our territory is ocean, and for this very reason, we are very proud to have co-facilitated together with Australia the year-long negotiations that led us to the consensual adoption of the Nice UNOC III Declaration. The SDGs are not abstract. They are about survival, dignity, and justice. They will lead us to a fairer world where no region, no country, no community, no individual is left behind. Let us translate the Abbas Agenda and the Pact for the Future into real, measurable progress for our people and our planet. Cabo Verde stands ready with resolve, with resilience, and with deep commitment to multilateralism to continue to work with all Member States, UN agencies, and global multi-stakeholders to make that future a reality. Obrigado. Thank you. And this ends the message of our Prime Minister. Thank you, Madam Presidente.

Madam Vice President, I have the honor to deliver the following statement on behalf of the Alliance of Small Island States, AOSIS. Today marks the one-year anniversary of the adoption of the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS, ABAS, by the General Assembly. For SIDS, ABAS is not just another inspirational document, it is a blueprint. It reflects the unique circumstances of SIDS, sets out a 10-year action plan, and outlines the support we need to achieve resilient prosperity. While we highlight the importance of the SDGs under review at this HLPF, for SIDS, our development story is not only about individual goals. Our challenges are interconnected. We cannot improve livelihoods without addressing debt burdens, and we cannot protect our oceans without access to finance and technology. This is why SIDS needs strategies that respond to our special circumstances, and it begins with partnerships. No matter how clearly SIDS articulate our priorities, without full support of the international community and adequate resources, we will continue to fall short. This is why SDG 17, the enabler, is especially critical. Coming out of the FFP4, the message is clear. The global financial architecture remains outdated. GDP per capita does not capture SIDS' unique vulnerabilities. We welcome the Sevilla Commitment as a shared commitment to close the gap between promises and progress in financing for development. Now is the time for delivery. Its full and effective implementation is critical to SIDS' efforts to achieve the ABAS and the SDGs. Its strong calls for the mainstreaming of the MDI to guide development policies and access to concessional finance and the operationalization of the Debt Sustainability Support Service highlights their centrality to unlocking the fiscal space SIDS urgently need. We also urge support for the full operationalization of the SIDS Center of Excellence. This is a key platform that will be driven by SIDS knowledge and will support data-driven solutions towards long-term resilience and prosperity. Last but not least, we must ensure that commitments on SDG 14 translate into action. For SIDS, the ocean is not just a resource, it is the bedrock of our identity, economy, and livelihoods. Madam Vice President, we have built the ABAS to be a roadmap. Now we call on the HLPF to play its role in accelerating progress in the implementation of our commitments. I thank you.

Thank you, Madame Vice President, Excellencies, distinguished panelists, delegates, dear friends. As a family of nations, the international community has the moral and political responsibility to support countries in special situations, including SIDS, in achieving sustainable development. Madam Vice President, debt remains one of the biggest obstacles to SIDS achieving the SDGs. Many SIDS are forced to spend more on serving debt than on public health or education. This situation conflicts with the commitments in the 2030 Agenda to pursuing sustainable development for all. Moreover, it is essential to recognize the ecological debt which exists particularly between the Global North and South, connected to commercial imbalances with effect on the environment and in disproportionate use of natural resources by certain countries over long periods of time, while poorer, more vulnerable nations, including SIDS, bear the brunt of climate impacts. This is not an economic issue, but a profoundly moral one too. In this context, there is an urgent need for immediate debt relief for SIDS and a comprehensive rethinking of the global debt architecture. Any reform must account for the vulnerability of SIDS, promote environmental justice, and prioritize the protection of human dignity. That relief alone is not a panacea. However, it has the potential to transform the development prospects of SIDS by providing them with the fiscal space to invest in essential pillars such as infrastructure, climate adaptation, health systems and education, which are crucial for SIDS to achieve sustainable development and resilient prosperity. Madam Vice President, with only 5 years left to achieve the SDGs, the international community must act with renewed urgency to free SIDS from the cycles of debt, disasters and delay they are facing. As Pope Leo Powerfully stated, the Jubilee which is being celebrated this year by the Catholic Church asks of us the restitution and redistribution of unjustly accumulated wealth as the way to personal and civil reconciliation. Thank you.
