In the spirit of partnership, we see the need to turn loss and damage funding into real access for grassroots and youth-led initiatives, especially in the frontline seats. It is also critical that issues and policies are being viewed and shaped through the youth lenses because challenges transform with the changing of time. They should be at the table. If not—
I thank the Major Group for Children and Youth for his statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Thailand, followed by Jamaica.

Thank you, Madam Chair. While accelerating SDGs implementation is on the agenda of every country, a special attention should be paid to Small Islands Developing States, or SIDS. Thailand, as an active emerging donor, has been promoting South-South and triangular cooperation to advance economic and social development guided by the 2030 Agenda. Despite geographical distance, Thailand has embraced its global responsibility for promoting development cooperation across the globe, not only in Southeast Asia, but as far as sits Thailand. In partnership with UNFPA and Timor-Leste, we carried out a Thai-Angola development project in maternal and reproductive health. The partnership boosts capacity of public health and hence contributed to SDG 3, good health and well-being. Moreover, an invitation has been sent to members of SIDS for training course and a postgraduate program in climate change mitigation and adaptation, ecotourism, and community development, all of which are attended by SIDS on an annual basis. The said capacity building scheme does only strengthen the capacity of SIDS to cope with issues that pose a challenge to sustainable development, but also contribute to an effort to enhance international partnership for the achievement of the 2030 Agenda. So to conclude, Thailand reaffirms its commitment to strengthening partnership at all forms with CEDAW to help them overcome challenges and enhance the efforts for SDG implementation. I thank you.
Thank you. I thank the distinguished representative of Thailand for her statement, and I now give the floor to distinguished representative of Jamaica.

Thank you, Madam Vice President, distinguished representatives. The adoption of the ABAS represents a significant milestone in our sustainable development journey. It offers a valuable roadmap for advancing sustainable development while building our inherent strengths and addressing our unique circumstances. The successful implementation of the ABAS demands more than high-level commitments. It requires translating policy prescriptions into field-level actions and delivering tangible outcomes for our communities. This transformation necessitates sustained international support, innovative financing mechanisms, and robust partnerships. Jamaica's commitment to the ABAS is reflected in our leadership within AOSIS and our national strategies prioritizing climate resilience, disaster risk financing, blue economy development, and renewable energy transition. SIDS, ladies and gentlemen, are not merely vulnerable states. SIDS are innovators pioneering solutions that the world urgently needs. The blue economy represents a transformative development model for SIDS, addressing equity in access to ocean resources, sharing benefits from marine assets, and offering the opportunity for reinvestment in human development and debt alleviation. Complementing our ocean-based innovations, digital transformation initiatives across SIDS are bridging geographic isolation through e-governance, telemedicine, distance learning, and geospatial data platforms. These developments demonstrate that innovation transcends transcends boundaries and that our perceived limitations can become competitive advantages in this digital age. Regional and international partnerships remain fundamental to our success. Financing remains among our greatest challenge. Caribbean states, for example, face critically high debt levels that constrain national budgets and available financing for sustainable development, climate change adaptation, and disaster risk reduction. The establishment of dedicated SIDS funding windows within multilateral climate funds is improving our access to concessional financing, and we continue to advocate for SIDS-specific criteria that recognize our unique circumstances

I thank the distinguished representative of Jamaica for her statement, and I remind you all that we only have 3 minutes per intervention. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ireland, followed by the— let me check that again. Ireland, you have the floor.

Thank you, Chair, distinguished speakers and colleagues. The Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS sets a clear trajectory towards resilient sustainable development, but the need for us all to take action on implementation is urgent. Let me highlight a few focus areas for Ireland in our ongoing collaboration with SIDS partners. First, on climate finance-related quality and accessibility issues, we're delighted that SIDS will have an allocation of at least 50% in the startup phase of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, on which we share a board seat. We believe there is potential to be explored in other funds for enhanced, accessible, and targeted support. Elsewhere, this month Ireland will provide €2 million to the Special Climate Change Fund SIDS window, which plays an essential role in supporting climate adaptation where it's needed most. Data and statistics are force for raising revenue, managing debt, unlocking investment, and they're essential for evidence-based policymaking. Ireland is working with UNDESA to support data governance and management in SIDS, with 3 country-led pilot projects underway in the Pacific, Caribbean, and AIS regions. We welcome work undertaken by the Secretariat on the monitoring and evaluation framework and look forward to feedback from the validation exercise. This is an important step in delivering a workable and effective tool for tracking progress and holding all of us to account in our implementation efforts. We look forward to similar progress on operationalisation— operationalisation of the MVI and the Centre of Excellence, including the debt sustainability support service, and we were pleased to see that highlighted in the Sevilla commitment. Genuine and effective partnership can drive change. Ireland will continue to contribute to the improvement of the partnership framework and global business network, as well as building on our bilateral ocean research partnerships, scholarships, and mobility awards. Chair, to conclude, let me reaffirm Ireland's commitment to collaboration with SIDS partners and relevant actors to ensure that the momentum we all felt at the conference just over a year ago is sustained in this critical phase. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Ireland, and I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Dominican Republic.

Thank you, Madam President, and thanks to the panelists for their presentations. With only 5 years left to achieve the 2030 Agenda, it is crucial that we stress the specific challenges faced by by small island developing states given their special situation. The Dominican Republic wants to make the most of the results from recent processes, UNOC 3 and FFD 4, to make progress effectively on its objectives. As a small island developing state, our country prioritizes marine ecosystems and climate resilience through initiatives such as the Office Against Sargassum, the expansion of protected areas, and coastal monitoring. Moreover, we promote regional and international partnerships to improve cooperation, highlight vulnerabilities, and to put the priorities of SIDS on the global agenda. We participate actively in mechanisms such as SICA, the Central American Integration System, addressing subjects such as biodiversity, sargassum management, and the energy transition. Despite this progress, we still face gaps in the implementation of the SDGs and consequently the ABAS as well. The lack of up-to-date and disaggregated data limits monitoring. There are still problems of inter-institutional coordination and limits in statistics systems. This affects the quality and timely nature of data. Therefore, it is essential that there be investment in resilient statistics infrastructure and that we promote open data frameworks. The Dominican Republic has made progress on this subject and we encourage the international community to recognize the multiplying impact generated by investing in platforms such as the SIDS Center for Excellence. This is particularly true when it comes to sustainability and making the most of the opportunities resulting from capacity building, above all when it comes to data generation. Moreover, the Dominican Republic has made progress in implementing the National Integrated Financing Framework. This is a central instrument for financing the SDGs., and it is backed up with tools such as the policy priority inference and practices such as budget tagging and multi-year planning. Lastly, we also have to mention the importance of incorporating the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index in the policies of multilateral banks, international organizations, and international financial institutions. This is a complement to help to forecast, address, and mitigate risks in a better informed way and to achieve aligned and inclusive development. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of the Dominican Republic for her statement, and I give the floor to the International Atomic Energy Agency, followed by Timo Lechte. Madam Chair, Excellency, colleagues.

Following on the commitment set by CEEDES IV last year, the International Atomic Energy Agency remains determined to support CEEDES countries to realize their Sustainable Development Goals. Our technical cooperation program support member states in key areas such as monitoring ocean activity, active education, managing marine resources, and addressing the impact of the microplastic. Within its New Tech Plastic Flagship initiative, the IEA has supported development of hammer— harmonized protocol and standardized methodologies now being applied by more than 20 SEAS countries to conduct national sampling and monitoring. Initial results expected later this year. Water resources management, where the agency can support SEAS in assessing and protecting the freshwater resources. Energy security and low-carbon development, where the IAEA can provide its expertise on grid integration and energy planning to enhance clean energy transition, including nuclear power and small modular reactor as a clean energy option to reduce dependence on fossil fuels. Food security and, and safety— IAEA cooperates with FAO using nuclear technology to improve agricultural productivity, combat pests like fruit flies, and ensure food safety through irradiation. And in public health sectors, IAEA supports low- and middle-income countries to enhance its capacity in radiation medicine against cancer by Rays of Hope Initiative, including small island nations with limited healthcare infrastructure. The IAEA stands ready to depend— depend on— deepen its partnership with these countries, ensuring that their voice can be heard, their needs are met, and their sustainable features are secured. I thank you very much.
I thank the representative of the International Atomic Energy Agency, and I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Timor-Leste, followed by Portugal.

Thank you, Madam President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen. For Small Island Developing States like Timor-Leste, the journey towards the Sustainable Development Goals is shaped by vulnerability, but also by determination and vision. The Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS is not just a roadmap; it is a moral imperative for us. Aligned with the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework, ABAS is fully embedded in our National Strategic Development Plan, which was central to our 2023 Voluntary National Review. Our challenges are real and interwoven, with climate shocks threatening our coastal communities, dependence on oil and gas, and persistent inequalities. Yet these are, these are also catalysts for transformation. Facing one of the Southeast Asia's highest rates of child malnutrition, Timor-Leste launched an evidence-based investment case for SDG 2, Zero Hunger. This whole-of-society strategy tackles food insecurity by integrating health, agriculture, social protection, and clean water. We are also pushing for inclusive growth. Our gender-responsive public procurement policies support women-led businesses, and our youth, our greatest resource, are being equipped through expanded technical, digital, and entrepreneurial training. Timor-Leste's identity as a SEEDS is not confined to geography, but defined by resilience and solidarity. Our recent accession to ASEAN and membership in the WTO mark a new chapter opening trade for Timor-Leste coffee, attracting responsible investment, and harmonizing national goals with regional priorities, especially in climate adaptation and the blue economy. In closing, Timor-Leste remains firmly committed to the 2030 Agenda. We are transforming vulnerabilities into opportunities through innovation, equity, and partnership. Let us continue to build bridges between nations and among people as we forge a resilient and prosperous future for all seeds. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Timor-Leste and I give the floor to the distinguished representative, permanent representative of Portugal.

Muchas gracias, señora presidenta. Thank you very much, Madam President. Thanks to the moderator, panelists, and discussant for their thoughtful contributions. Portugal is a longstanding partner of CEEDES. We fully support the Antigua and Barbuda agenda for CEEDES and welcome this opportunity to to highlight early efforts to implement it. Let me share with you 3 brief points. First, data. Data is the backbone of implementation. We must invest in national statistical systems and platforms for knowledge sharing. Portugal is doing so with SEEDS partners like Cape Verde, São Tomé and Príncipe, and Timor-Leste. Second, we need to turn commitments into actions. At UNOC III, we committed to protecting 20%— 27% of our sea, including 30% around the Azores, ratified the BB&J agreement, and announced the launch of a new edition of the Portugal-UN Oceans Fellowship. At FFD IV, we joined the 4P Roadmap for Better Inclusion of the MVI and co-organized a high-level event calling, among other things, for the constitution of the independent expert advisory panel foreseen in Resolution 78/322 on the MVI, which Antigua and Barbuda and Portugal co-facilitated. We also showcased in other high-level events how debt-for-climate swaps and triangular cooperation can accelerate SDGs implementation in SEEDS. Third and finally, effective follow-up mechanisms matter. Strengthening the steering committee for SEEDS partnerships and the global business network is key to ensuring AVAS delivers results. We look forward to considering the recommendations recently circulated to the membership in the GA. Portugal remains firmly committed to the implementation of AVAS. With seeds and for seeds. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Portugal for his statement, and I now give the floor to the International Development Law Organization. Over to you.

Thank you, Chair. The adoption of the 2030 Agenda gave us a roadmap to a more prosperous future.. But as we've heard time and again, we are not on track to deliver what was promised in 2015. Abbas, however, provides an opportunity to reinvigorate sustainable development efforts and encourage us not only to focus our determination on the next 5 years, but beyond 2030. IDLO welcomes in this regard Abbas's reaffirmation of the rule of law and justice as a catalyst for peaceful, prosperous, and inclusive societies, and the importance of building strong institutions as well as gender equality. Following this, let me share 3 ways in which strengthening the rule of law and advancing SDG 16 can help us achieve common goals in the 2030 Agenda and ABUS. First, progress on SDG 16 can promote inclusive economic growth. IDLO works with governments to enhance regulatory frameworks, build capacity to resolve commercial disputes, and protect national assets while strengthening investor confidence. These are key in creating an enabling economic environment that builds trust and generates resources that can be reinvested in sustainable development efforts. Second, the rule of law provides a framework for the integrated solutions needed to deliver the SDGs and ABUS. As we confront existing and new challenges, from climate change to digital transformation, we need effective legal frameworks and accountable institutions to ensure that policy ambitions translate into results. Third, the rule of law is a powerful enabler of women's empowerment across SIDS. Eliminating discriminatory laws and adopting transformative legal frameworks that combat violence and economic exclusion are critical ingredients in facilitating the participation and leadership of women in public life and ultimately closing the gap. IDLO stands ready to partner with you in advancing the rule of law and access to justice on your journey to 2034, and I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of International Development Law Organization for his statement. I have the honor to give the floor to the distinguished representative of Spain, followed by New Zealand and Finland. Spain, you have the floor.

Thank you very much, Madam President. Spain participated last year in the 4th Conference on SIDS in St. Johns and welcome the adoption of the Abbas. We believe that it is an agenda that has a strong link to its predecessors and establishes a clear blueprint for, uh, the, um, next decade and, and gives clear responses to the many vulnerabilities and challenges faced by these countries. In its— in, in their main goals, it have the full support of our country. Spain welcomes— I would like to underscore the valuable contributions made by SIDS at the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development that we have just hosted in Sevilla. The conclusions and proposals made on financing that emanated, that resulted from the Antigua and Barbuda and Sevilla meetings are, in our view, consistent and strengthen one another. We also reiterate that the mobilization of resources is critical to ensure that SIDS can achieve the SDGs. In that regard, capacity building is crucial. And so is mobilizing domestic resources and the role of the private sector in order to promote sustainable and inclusive investments that encourage economic diversification. We also point to issues that Spain has consistently stressed, such as greater effort made by international cooperation to build resilience, early warning systems, and disaster risk reduction, as well as strengthening climate action with a focus on adaptation. In that regard, I would mention by way of an example the fact that the Spanish Cooperation Agency has just signed a new commitment with Cabo Verde for budgetary support for sustainable development in the blue economy. Moreover, in the framework of FFD negotiations, Spain clearly has opted for strengthened commitments in the area of rechanneling special drawing rights and when it comes to debt sustainability, as well as in favor of the systematic and standardized inclusion in loans of debt pause clauses that make it possible to automatically suspend debt payment in the case of predetermined shocks such as natural disasters, food crises, or pandemics. Tax— robust tax systems must also be established, and international tax cooperation needs to be strengthened to also address illicit financial flows. Moreover, the reality of SIDS and the multidimensional nature of their challenges means that we need to make progress on metrics and indicators that go beyond GDP, including the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index. And in that regard, we are working to advance the adoption of metrics that go beyond average income, and we will continue to drive forward considerations and debates in the OECD and the United Nations also when it comes to the multidimensional nature of the FFD agenda that has just been given an important boost in the Sabiha Conference. Therefore, we believe that partnerships the best way to make progress in— and in that regard, countries can count on our support to make progress in implementing the Abbas. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Spain, and I have the pleasure to give the floor to the distinguished representative of New Zealand, followed by Finland and Italy. Distinguished Ambassador, you have the floor.

Thank you, Chair. New Zealand has a longstanding commitment to work with Small Island Developing States to support their voice and their leadership as they advance their sustainable development, including through full implementation of the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS. New Zealand was honored to co-chair this process along with Maldives. There are many strategies that SIDS take to achieve the SDGs, including those we have heard about today, from addressing climate to ocean governance in financing, MVI, debt sustainability, to name a few. But we thought it would be helpful today to focus on the role that regionalism can play. And we acknowledge up front that the SIDS regions have variability when it comes to regional architecture, but we thought it would be useful to show you as a case study what we do in the Pacific when it comes to regionalism. The Pacific works together at a political level to agree sustainable development priorities for the region. These are outlined in the Pacific Island Forum's 2050 strategy for the Blue Pacific continent. Regional approaches also play a key role in the delivery of development cooperation, with Pacific regional agencies supporting countries in a wide range of important technical functions, helping Pacific SIDS to overcome the inherent challenges they face with size. New Zealand invests heavily in regional architecture on the basis of this philosophy that it is Pacific-led and Pacific-owned. We all know that SIDS themselves, all of them, face unique vulnerabilities as small, remote, and geographically dispersed countries. But what I think is more difficult for us as the international community is to take the next step as their international partners partners to respond to those vulnerabilities by adapting our usual policies and our usual processes for international cooperation. Only then can we ensure that those are SIDS-led and SIDS-owned. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of New Zealand. I would now like to give the floor to Finland, to be followed by Italy and China.

Thank you, Miss Chair, Excellencies, sustainability friends. Congratulations to SIDS on the adoption and the initial implementation of the ABAS. Finland acknowledges that the Small Island Developing States face unique challenges from sea level rise, extreme weather to coral reef degradation, limited land, and of course, lack of sufficient financing. SIDS also offer important opportunities and perspectives for sustainable development, local engagement, and innovation. I myself live on the Åland Islands in the heart of the Baltic Sea. The Åland Islands The Åland Islands are an autonomous region of Finland. The autonomy is more than 100 years old and we have been demilitarized since the mid-19th century. A year ago, we submitted an SDG voluntary review to the UN entitled Everyone Can Flourish on the Islands of Peace. In this document, we share our 10 years of experiences from SDG implementation and introduced the Everyone Can Flourish vision, philosophy, and associated governance model. And relatedly, Åland aims to ensure that everyone possesses equal freedom and influence in shaping society and their own destinies. So we are of course ready and willing to collaborate with like-minded individuals and organizations. Regarding Finland's international development cooperation, disaster risk prevention is an important element. We finance initiatives in developing countries that support Early Warnings for All, the initiative of the UN Secretary-General. And Finland is a forerunner and reliable partner in efforts to build resilience. For many years, we have financed the improvement of weather climate services to over 50 national meteorological and hydrological services around the globe during the past decade. Through Finland's ongoing cooperation, improved weather climate services and early warning systems benefit over 700 million people, and inclusive early warning systems enhance the resilience of entire communities. Finally, Finland emphasizes the importance of gender-responsive services, recognizing that climate change aggravates existing inequalities affecting women's access to resources, safety, and health services. Thank you very much. Finland.
Thank you, thank you, Finland. I give the floor to Italy, to be followed by China.

Our discussion today is particularly important in light of the current transformative moment of the UN agenda, with important events and conferences and processes which are redefining the priorities and the functioning of mechanism which Small Island Developing Countries rely. Just recently, at UNOC 2023, Italy submitted 13 voluntary commitments aimed at the protection and sustainable use of the ocean and seas for a total amount of €150 million. Italy remains committed to the implementation of the Antigua-Barbuda Agenda for Seas. As we said, first of all, it is essential that the means of implementation that we will devise together are responsive to the specific needs and the specific, specific circumstances of Indeed, vulnerability must not just be a recognition of fragility. It should rather be assessed to provide more support to build resilience. The MVI is one such support measure. Second, partnerships are crucial, as well as blended finance and a renewed commitment by countries in a position to do so to raise the ambition of our carbon neutrality goals. Third, We heard Sid's calls during the FFD4 negotiations. We must do more to integrate the climate and development agenda. Coming to climate finance, Italy is committed to do its part. The Italian Climate Fund, with a €4.4 billion budget in its revolving nature, is currently the biggest of this kind. Besides financing, the cultural and creative sector remain a priority for the diversification of Sid's economies. In this regard, we must identify solutions and innovations that are tailored to the realities of SEEDS and aligned to objectives such as social equity, environmental protection, and long-term prosperity. Italy is accompanying the ABAS process and implementation also through our longstanding multilateral partnership frameworks with the Pacific SEEDS and the CARICOM, the Caribbean one, that have been operating since 2015 and which we have recently updated and broadened in scope to make them in line with EABAS. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Italy for her statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of China, followed by the Scientific and Technological Community Major Group. China origin.

Madam President, in recent years, SIDS have made huge efforts to achieve socioeconomic development and address climate change. But they still face multiple challenges such as lack of diversity in economic structure, shortage of funds for development, and frequent climate-related disasters. Last year, the 4th International Conference on SIDS was held successfully. The international community should vigorously implement ABAS and scale up targeted support to SIDS. First, development must be given priority. More input must flow to SIDS in the field of infrastructure, trade and investment, and marine economy. Regarding the multidimensional vulnerability of SIDS, systematic solutions have to be found. The developed countries and multilateral development agencies must provide SIDS with more development resources in support of their implementation of the 2030 Agenda. Second, support must be lent to SIDS in tapping their development potential, bringing into full play their rich resources and comparative advantages, diversifying their economic structure, promoting employment, and improving people's livelihood. At the same time, it is imperative to strengthen technological and digital empowerment, upgrade industrial transformation, and enhance capabilities for self-development. Third, it is necessary to support SIDS in addressing climate change, adhere to the goals and principles of UNFCCC and its Paris Agreement, and help SIDS boost their capacity and resilience in the face of climate change. The developed countries must honor their commitments in earnest and adequately support SIDS in finance, technology, and capacity building. Certain major powers' withdrawal from the Paris Agreement runs counter to the aspirations of SIDS. China has been firmly supporting the development of SIDS through such mechanisms as the China-CELAC Cooperation Forum and the China-Pacific Island Countries Economic Development and Cooperation Forum, among others. China has carried out concrete cooperation with SIDS under the framework of the Global Development Initiative. China and SIDS have jointly established such platforms as the Climate Change Center and the Center of Excellence for agricultural cooperation with a view to benefiting the local community. We stand ready to work with all to actively support SIDS in accelerating the implementation of the 2030 Agenda towards lasting prosperity with greater resilience. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of China, Xie Xinyi. I now give the floor to distinguished representative of the Scientific and Technological Community Major Group, followed by France and Papua New Guinea.

Thank you, Madam Vice President, and distinguished delegates. I am honored to speak on behalf of the Scientific and Technological Community Major Group, co-coordinated by the International Science Council and the World Federation of Engineering Organizations. I have the pleasure to share a message today from our SIDS Committee. This is a group of scientists from across SIDS who are working to strengthen science systems and capacity in their countries. And regions. As SIDS move from commitment to implementation under the ABAS, we stress three urgent imperatives from the scientific community. First, the persistent disconnect between donor priorities and local needs must be resolved. Scientific and engineering priorities in SIDS are too often shaped by external funding agendas. ABAS implementation must be informed by science that is both locally grounded and globally visible. This includes greater investment in indigenous knowledge systems and locally-led research, especially in areas like climate adaptation, biodiversity protection, and food and water security. Second, monitoring and evaluation of ABAS cannot succeed without addressing the foundational data and capacity challenges in SIDS. We call for concrete support for national science commissions, regional academies, and knowledge-sharing platforms of all kinds in order to build sustained institutional capacity. Third, SIDS are not only sites of vulnerability, as has been underlined during this session, but true front-runners in innovation. Their natural endowments and adaptive capacities should be leveraged in partnerships that treat SIDS as leaders and co-designers, not just recipients of scientific, engineering and technological development. In closing, we urge the UN system and its member states to provide predictable long-term support for SIDS-led science and engineering, including through the proposed SIDS Centre of Excellence. Let us move beyond rhetorical inclusion to genuine co-production of knowledge in large ocean states. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Scientific and Technological Community, Major group for her statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of France, followed by Papua New Guinea and Germany. France, over to you.

Madam President, ladies and gentlemen, small island developing states, SIDS, face social, economic, and environmental risks that are very specific. They're seeing rising sea levels, dwindling marine resources, the acidification of oceans, the list goes on. France remains determined to fully incorporate the vulnerabilities these states face into the multilateral response across all fronts. The Institute of Development Research, on behalf of which I'm taking the floor today, deems this multidimensional vulnerability necessary to to be recognized. This requires an interdisciplinary global scientific approach underpinned by the science of sustainability. In order to be operational and effective, the vulnerability study of ecosystems requires tools which are fit for purpose for data collection and analysis. This requires methodological research. So that we can come up with new protocols and new ways of sampling, new ways of conducting statistical analysis into Aelia. All of this must be adapted to the context of insular ecosystems. The development of solutions, especially as regards climate change adaptation, requires us to craft various models which are tailored to the size of these islands. Working hand in hand with the Institute of Research for Development, we would like to draw your attention to the need to co-build research programs working with local actors emphasizing issues such as multivector disease, health, and so on. Risk adaptation, volcanic and seismic, All of this is being heightened by climate change and therefore exacerbating vulnerability. Loss of marine and land biodiversity— this is something we must address and protect. Social, economic, and migratory studies must underpin land management policies. I thank you, Madam President.

I think that the single representative of France for his statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Papua New Guinea, followed by Germany and FAO. Madam President and Mr. Moderator, thank you for guiding this welcome and timely dialogue to support the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for Seeds, which we see as a crucial framework to deliver on the seeds sustainable development needs, including their specific vulnerabilities. This deserves real, practical support from the international community at speed and scale. Let me also thank the respective panelists for the thoughtful presentations, and may I especially pay tribute to Papua New Guinea's very own panelist, Ruth Kissam, who has been a woman's leader and a champion for our country in the context of marshalling our civil society and other multi-stakeholders in our national development efforts, and for her stirring message shared. Madam President, at the 4th International Conference on Financing for Development in Spain, my delegation underscored that financing is not just an important development tool. It is pivotal for the delivery of the SDGs and more importantly, making positive difference to the lives and livelihoods of our peoples on a sustained basis. For SIDS, without adequate, timely and predictable financing, the 2030 Agenda remains out of reach. For SIDS, our challenges of limited fiscal space, debt vulnerability, constrained access to climate finance and an unresponsive global financial system are deeply interconnected. The ABAS responds directly to these realities. Madam President, let me share with you two examples. The first one is in relation to climate financing. This year, last month, Papua New Guinea hosted the Green Climate Fund Board meeting. We submitted a proposal 9 years ago and just in June we got approval for that proposal. This is not how we should deal with climate financing. It is the antithesis of the Abbas and the Sevilla de compromiso agenda. Secondly, on financing the debt issues. Last Friday, my Prime Minister met with the IMF Deputy Director-General and the message was loud and clear: we have to do better to support SIDS and it is not good enough in what we are doing on climate financing and all other aspects. This needs to be taken into account properly. In conclusion, we appeal to the international community to support the SIDS deliver on ABAS. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Papua New Guinea for his statement, and I now give the floor to Germany, followed by FAO and Suriname. Germany, over to you.

Excellencies, colleagues, at the outset, let me thank the chair, the keynote speaker, the moderator, the panelists, and the discussion for the very rich insights. As it was mentioned by many previous speakers, We have a stock of critical documents that were adopted throughout the last couple of months. First and foremost, the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS, the UNOC III, and the FFD outcome documents in particular. The focus must now lie on implementation. Going forward, genuine and effective partnerships will be key. Partnerships to foster access to finance, capacity building, and knowledge, knowledge exchange amongst others. Germany remains committed to collaborating closely with SIDS to address these issues. Allow me to highlight 3 brief examples of Germany's engagement. First, ranging from climate resilient initiatives to economic and technical assistance in the Pacific and in the Caribbean alone, the German International Climate Initiative is funding close to 40 bilateral, regional, and global projects programs, projects, and partnerships with a volume of up to €700 million. Second, as the first donor to the Rising Nations Initiative, Germany aims to protect Pacific atoll countries' statehood and sovereignty while safeguarding affected populations' rights and their rich cultural heritage. And third and lastly, we fully agree with the assessment that the availability and effective use of Data is key to unlocking progress towards achieving the SDGs and implementing ABAS, as it has been reflected extensively by the panelists. In that regard, Germany is proud to be working closely with Antigua and Barbuda to finalize our contribution to the SIDS Center of Excellence and the SIDS Global Data Hub. Excellencies, colleagues, the next few years are crucial to making significant progress. Progress. Therefore, let us work together on the full implementation of the Abas and achieving the SDGs. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Germany for his statement. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of FAO, followed by Suriname and Nauru. FAO, over to you.

Gracias, señora presidenta. Excellencies, colleagues, and partners. Small Island Developing States are among the most vulnerable countries in the world. They are facing a convergence of challenges: increasing intensity and frequency of climate shocks, rising sea levels, limited arable land and freshwater resources, and high dependence on imported food. Over 70% of the population in SIDS lives in coastal areas, leaving communities and in agrifood systems dangerously exposed to hurricanes, saltwater intrusion, and flooding. Agriculture, fisheries, and forests the backbone of rural livelihoods, are under intense pressure. In many SIDS, more than 80% of food is imported, driving up costs and weakening local food production. At the same time, transport and infrastructure constraints raise the cost of both importing and exporting local products, limiting competitiveness and deepening food insecurity. The cost of the healthy diet in SIDS is among the highest globally, and 1 in 5 people also face moderate or severe fear of food insecurity. In this context, FAO plays a critical role in transforming agrifood systems. We support SIDS in developing and implementing national strategies that are tailored to their unique geographies, economies, and vulnerabilities. This includes policy advice, technical assistance, and investment planning anchored in data and science. The Hands in Hands initiative, which uses advanced geospatial modeling to target investments in areas with the highest potential for transformation, is now active in over a dozen SIDS. Our Blue Transformation Agenda supports the sustainable development of aquatic food systems vital for SIDS where fish account for over 50% of annual protein intake and offer huge potential for value chain development and export earnings. At the same time, FAO promotes innovation across sectors—climate-smart agriculture, digital technologies for farmers, and frontier research including microbiome science to enhance productivity and sustainability. In many SIDS, post-harvest food loss reaches up to 30%, especially in perishable commodities. Reducing this loss is essential to improving food security. FAO is also working to unlock finance for smallholder and rural entrepreneurs. We promote better targeting of public investment while also engaging in private and blended finance to scale up impact. Strengthening partnerships with government, civil society, research institutions, and the private sector— is essential to building resilience and ensuring no one is left behind. In closing, the path to SDG success in SID runs through transformed agrifood systems, ones that are productive, sustainable, climate resilient, and nutrition sensitive. FAO remains fully committed to supporting SIDS in building this future, one that nourishes people, sustains ecosystems, and leaves no one behind. Thank you very much. I made it this time.
I thank the distinguished representative of FAO for her statement. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Suriname, followed by Nauru and the Sovereign Order of Malta.

Thank you, Madam Chair, and also appreciation to the moderator and the panelists for their contribution. Madam Chair, the Republic of Suriname, as a low-lying coastal state, joins CARICOM and consists in urging that the ABAs must deliver real transformative change for our people, not just promises on paper. We welcome the powerful remarks of the SG of the UN, who reminded the world in Antigua and Barbuda that SIDS are a test case for climate and financial justice and that we cannot face these challenges alone. We echoed his call. The international community has a duty to stand with us. For Suriname, strengthening ABAS means confronting three core realities. First, time is not on our side. With just five years left to achieve the SDGs, our people need urgent and concrete solutions. This includes fair access to financing, debt relief, and partnerships that reflect our real vulnerabilities and development needs. Second, many SIDS continue to face barriers to affordable and accessible financing. We must ensure that resources flow where they are needed the most, namely to build resilient communities, protect natural ecosystems, and unlock inclusive sustainable growth. Third, we cannot manage what we cannot measure. For ABAS to succeed, To succeed, we must close persistent data gaps, invest in stronger national statistical systems, and share knowledge across our region. Reliable data is key to accountability and adapting to what works. We also view the Pact for the Future as an important agreement and critical opportunity to reinforce these ambitions. It must support ABAS by securing practical means of implementation and not just renewed promises, but tangible support that SIDS can depend on. In closing, Suriname stands with our fellow SIDS and the SG in calling for ABAS to remain a living document, one that is driven by our priorities, owned by our communities, and backed by genuine international solidarity and support. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Suriname for her statement. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Nauru, followed by the sovereign owner of Malta and UN-Habitat. Nauru, over to you.

Thank you, Madam Chair, and to the Moderator and panel. Nauru aligns with the statements delivered by the distinguished representatives for the Alliance of Small Island States and the Pacific Small Island Developing States. With just 5 years until 2030, our national report shows we are behind across every target—basic health, education, water and sanitation, infrastructure, and climate resilience. Despite this reality, Nauru is set to graduate to high-income status by 2026. The outcomes of UNOC 3 and FFD 4 must translate into action. We need financing frameworks that respond to real-world vulnerability, not just income per capita. Graduation should reflect development progress and the MVI used to guide access to finance. Data systems remain weak, under-resourced, and heavily dependent on external technical support. We cannot track SDG progress or inform good policymaking without investing in core national statistics capacity. We strongly support the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SEEDS, initiatives like the SEEDS Data Hub, but we need sustained support. Partnerships rely on strong regional and multilateral collaboration, whether through the Pacific Islands Forum, the UN system, or bilateral partners, to bridge resource and capacity gaps. Partnerships must be grounded in trust and continue to amplify National voices. Financing we urgently need, tailored to SIDS realities. Current models reward credit ratings and income status, systems where SIDS, like Nauru, are already excluded. Climate finance is increasingly hard to access. Costs are going up, entry points are narrowing, and the burden is growing. In fact, we are structurally vulnerable and economically fragile. Colleagues, graduation should not be the start of a crisis. Let us use the outcomes of UNOC 3, FFD 4, and this HLPF to build a system that works with SIDS, that gives us the tools to reach the Sustainable Development Goals. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Nauru for her statement. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Sovereign Order of Malta, followed by UN-Habitat and the LGBTI stakeholder group. Over to you, sir.

Madam Chair, distinguished panel and moderator, sustainable development and sovereignty go go hand in hand. Our focus this afternoon is on sustainable development in the context of climate change and sovereignty, or in other words, identity. The Sovereign Order of Malta does not speak of displaced peoples and the loss of territorial integrity as an abstract, distant abstraction. We speak as an institution that has for over two centuries continued its unique sovereign mission without a land to call its own. When our land— when we were expelled from the island of Malta, our sovereignty seemed lost. Yet through the ensuing 227 years, we have survived, not through force, but through international recognition, through our own belief in our potentials for survival, and with the help and support of others. Building on this legacy, we continue to exercise a functional sovereignty through diplomatic relations with 115 states that stands as proof that sovereignty does not have to be rooted in land, but in recognition, the will to survive, and a moral purpose that gives it life. Our history speaks directly to the crisis now confronting Small Island Developing States. For many SIDS, territorial loss is not hypothetical, it is becoming a reality. Shorelines retreat, homes vanish, legal status trembles. But what does not recede is identity, purpose, nor dignity. These are not held in the ground beneath one's feet, but in the will of a people to endure, and affirm their right to exist as autonomous communities. We have seen the hardships of our own history echoed in some ways in the lived reality of others today. In Tuvalu, a government prepares to preserve its nationhood in the cloud, building a digital replica of its identity, institutions, and cultural heritage, not as an innovation project, but as a dramatic measure to ensure continuity when land may no longer remain, yet a vision and a culture does. In the Maldives, the world's first floating city is under construction, not as a luxury development but as a humanitarian and constitutional safeguard in anticipation of rising seas. As our own history reveals, sovereignty can survive the loss of land, but only when accompanied by recognition and oftentimes reinvention and innovation. What we learn through survival must now inform the world's response to those—
I thank the distinguished representative of the Sovereign Order of Malta for his statement, and I now give the floor to UN-Habitat, followed by the LGTBI stakeholder group and UNICEF.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, colleagues. UN-Habitat is honored to address on global progress on advancing sustainable development in small island development states. UN-Habitat calls the development partners to reaffirm our commitment to the 2030 Agenda and the New Urban Agenda, recognizing the urgent need to accelerate sustainable urban development in SIDS. Urbanization in these territories presents both challenges and transformative opportunities for inclusive, resilient, and climate-smart development. Strengthened support is needed to voluntary local reviews, local climate action plans, and inclusive municipal planning to localize the SDGs and improve service delivery to the communities in small island state— in small island states. National urban policies and housing strategies must be updated and integrated into climate and NDC frameworks to ensure their coherent multi-sectoral implementation. We also need advocacy on expanding adaptation-focused urban initiatives such as slum upgrading, nature-based solutions, and loss and damage assessments aligned with the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda, emphasizing resilience, equity, and climate finance access. Development partners must commit to embedding the principles of the APAS and the Pacific Nuban Agenda and the 2050 Strategy for the Blue Pacific Continent into all programming, promoting inclusion and multilevel partnerships. Regional platforms like the Pacific Urban Partnership and Pacific Urban Forum must be leveraged to foster coordination, knowledge exchange, and joint action. As many others have said, we emphasize the importance of robust data systems, such as the Pacific Sustainable Development Indicators, to inform planning and decision-making at all levels. Finally, we call for expanded access to climate finance and urban investment to support transformative locally-led SDG initiatives. We invite all partners here to join us in advancing sustainable urbanization for cities. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of UN-Habitat for her statement, and I now give the floor to LGBTI stakeholder group. Followed by UNICEF.

Thank you, Madam President, and thank you, panelists, for your important and insightful contributions. I speak on behalf of the LGBTQI stakeholder group and bring the voice of Suriname, a Caribbean South American developing state and part of the wider regional struggle for inclusive and resilient development. In our region, where colonial legacies continue to shape laws, mindsets, and economies, LGBTQI people often face multiple layers of exclusion. In Suriname, LGBTQI youth report alarmingly high rates of suicidal thoughts, trans people are denied jobs based on their appearance, and families are forced to navigate legal systems that don't recognize their existence. These aren't isolated cases. They mirror experiences across many Caribbean islands. While the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS rightly emphasizes capacity building and enabling systems, we must ensure that these do not reproduce exclusion but actively dismantle it. For that, LGBTQI people must be at the table, not just as beneficiaries but as designers of solutions. We urge SIDS governments to ensure that national development strategies particularly those related to health, gender equality, decent work, and inclusive partnerships include LGBTQI realities and are informed by disaggregated data, local consultations, and lived experience. In Suriname, our court has taken bold steps to affirm LGBTI rights, but without legislative and executive follow-through, justice remains partial. We therefore call on Caribbean SIDS to integrate LGBTI inclusion in national action plans for SDGs, invest in disaggregated data and community-led solutions, ensure meaningful participation in LGBTQI organizations and policy processes. We call on the international community to back LGBTQI inclusion and SIDS with targeted funding, technical assistance, and space for regional cooperation. Decriminalization, legal protection, and community-led action are not luxuries. They are essential to achieving inclusive health, gender equality, decent work, and effective partnerships. Let us ensure that no one is left behind, not in policy, not in practice, and not in the path forward. Grantangi, thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of the GTBI stakeholder group for her statement. I now give the floor to UNICEF, followed by the UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction, the last speaker for today. Mic for UNICEF, please.

Gracias, señora presidenta. Thank you very much, Madam President. Distinguished delegates, as many have stated, small island developing states continue to face complex and overlapping challenges as they are at the crossroads of climate vulnerability, constrained fiscal space, and persistent development financing gaps. However, within SIDS, it is children who are paying the price for these challenges. SIDS account for less than 1% of global carbon emissions, but are amongst the most exposed to climate-related events. Since the 1970s, they have endured more than $150 billion in climate and weather-related losses. In the period between 2016 and 2021, over 43 million children, most of these in SIDS countries, were displaced by weather-related events. COVID-19 placed additional pressure on tourism-reliant economies, and many SIDS are now navigating high debt burdens that limit investment in the essential social services upon which children depend, such as health, education, and social protection. UNICEF remains committed to supporting governments across SIDS in the implementation of the Abbas to mitigate the effects of these crises by building systems that are more resilient to shocks, from digital education platforms in São Tomé e Príncipe, to climate-resilient WASH infrastructure in Vanuatu, to launching the world's first-ever integrated climate and disaster risk finance mechanism specifically targeted and designed to be effective for children and young people called Today and Tomorrow. Many of these solutions are laid out in UNICEF's SIDS position paper that we released last year. To build on these efforts, we see three areas where the international community can help accelerate progress. First, by protecting and scaling up development finance with greater attention to child outcomes, including ring-fencing budgets for child-focused essential services and investments in age and sex disaggregated data. Second, by promoting and implementing child-sensitive approaches to debt sustainability and relief. In particular, the debt pause clauses that were launched in Sevilla as well as other key commitments in El Compromiso de Sevilla. And third, by ensuring that climate adaptation and the implementation of the ABAs place children as key contributors to resilience and innovation, not as passive beneficiaries of support. Within the 5 years remaining to achieve the SDGs, we can implement many solutions if we keep our focus on children. The children in SIDS have already called for respect of all their rights, during the Abbas Child and Youth Action Summit. It is up to us to honor that call. Le doy las gracias.
I thank the distinguished representative of UNICEF for her statement. I now give the floor to the UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction. Over to you.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Small Island Developing States are amongst the most disaster-prone countries in the world. They face a disaster mortality rate more than double the global average and disaster costs that are amongst the highest in the world relative to the size of their economies. To reduce disaster losses and achieve resilient prosperity, it is essential for disaster risk reduction to be integrated in policies, programs, and investments at all levels in SIDS. The Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS makes clear the centrality of disaster risk reduction to sustainable development in SIDS with clear calls to action. With increasing frequency and intensity of disasters projected for the future, UNDRR is committed to supporting SIDS in shoring up their resilience in alignment with the Abbas and guided by the Geneva Call for Action emerging from the Global Platform for Disaster Risk Reduction held last month. This includes helping SIDS to enhance their capacity for data collection and prioritizing their needs under initiatives such as the UN Secretary-General's Early Warnings for All initiative and the Santiago Network for Averting, Minimizing, and Addressing Loss and Damage. In addition, we stand ready to support SIDS to stress test the resilience of their infrastructure systems and to support them in applying the principles resilient infrastructure. UNDRR also calls on the international community to provide the necessary means of implementation for the Abbas, including adequate funding for DRR elements, as also affirmed in the outcomes of FFD4. Current levels of disaster-related investment are not to the scale to meet the needs and continue to be skewed towards post-disaster response rather than proactive resilience building. As a result, SIDS often find themselves trapped in cycles of recovery with little room for resilience gains and sustainable development. In closing, UNDRR reaffirms its support to SIDS and the implementation of the ABAS in line with the targets and goal of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of UNDRR for his statement. We have heard the last speaker on the list. I will now give the floor back to the moderator in order to hear reflections from the panelists as well as to hear his own concluding remarks. Mr. Bishop, you have the floor.

Many thanks, everybody. Many thanks, Chair. We've heard a lot of very, very important comments this afternoon, and what I thought I would try to do is just distill them into a few broad insights that I think have come out of the conversation today, and then shape that into a final question that I'll ask to the panelists. The first one is that we keep hearing that the Abbas is a blueprint, it's a vision, it's a roadmap for the future, as was the 2030 process when it was established. And the question for us here maybe is how to render that vision, render that blueprint into something substantive. Another then is that the urgency of timely ABAS implementation is clear. The frameworks to achieve this are in the process of being developed, and they need to be implemented as rapidly as possible. But this needs more than just high-level commitments, as it was put by one respondent. There is a huge amount of importance in synergizing the ABAS with the SDGs and related processes as well. Another thing that a few people said is that SIDS vulnerability coexists with remarkable SIDS leadership. I don't actually think this is a surprise, and as someone who's taught small state studies in universities for a long time, I could digress into an academic conversation about why SIDS show such remarkable leadership, and it's precisely because of their vulnerability, in my view, but I'll resist that temptation today. There's a need for rapid unlocking of finance and other sources of support. This is something we've heard repeatedly. There's an ongoing challenge of indebtedness, both financial indebtedness and indebtedness to the environment, which is as much a moral issue as it is an economic one. There is potentially There is potential perhaps for SIDS to leapfrog some of their excellent development gaps and become competitiveness leaders in a digital age if the right technologies, infrastructures, and data sources are leveraged. Again, we've heard this quite a few times. Um, and then finally, the fact that children, young people, and other marginalized groups suffer most from the ongoing development challenges and gaps faced in SIDS. I don't think this is something we hear as much as we should, but we've certainly heard it a few times today. But that often these people, particularly young people, are those that are the first to support their societies without complaint when a crisis of some kind hits, and yet they're often the ones that bear the brunt of those crises. I could go on, but I won't. As I say, I've tried to condense all of this down into a simple question for the panellists, and we'll begin with Sergio, because I think it's important for Ambassador Sayed to have the last word. Here on today's panel as the chair of AOSIS. So we keep hearing, as I said just now, that the Abbas has provided a blueprint, but what, from your perspective, needs to happen now to implement it fully, to synergize it with other processes, and turn all of the positive words that we've heard from delegates here this afternoon into hard cash, substantive resources of other kinds, and action to really deliver resilient prosperity? So I hand the floor to you, Sergio.

Thank you so much, Matt. Thank you. I think, you know, what's exciting is that when we look at this blueprint, there is really an incredible opportunity to make the change. We see companies today that are moving in as non-state actors and trillions of dollars, but yet we see our countries and our small islands lacking that innovation. And I think the imperative here that we have with the ABIS Center of Excellence Global Data Hub and the evolution of technologies that now allow us to bring that capacity and that education to these small islands and help them leapfrog. It's one of the greatest opportunities in our lifetime. So I'll end with that. Thank you.
Fantastic. Ambassador Said.

Thank you so much, Mr. Moderator. Yes, I think the, the ABAS is the blueprint and the strategic roadmap is a clear one. And I think the first step that we're taking to establish the monitoring and evaluation framework is a very important one. One of our speakers said you can't measure— you can't manage what you don't measure. And I think that's key to make sure that we have the systems in place that allow us to monitor where we're going. So I think that's a key part of the implementation of the Plan. Again, finance is something that we've kind of reiterated over and over. But just to kind of touch on what our— my fellow panelists said on kind of the digital leapfrogging idea, I think this is a really exciting time for SIDS to be able to take that opportunity. SIDS are— it's kind of— we're seeing a new world emerge. I think digital infrastructure infrastructure. The cost of broadband used to be incredibly expensive, and now we have technologies like Starlink and other companies that allow internet access to even the remote— the most remote SIDS. And I think that's a really key development that we're seeing. We're seeing things, you know, SIDS are huge ocean economies. We struggle from IUU fishing, for example. If we capture the economic value of the fisheries that's taken from us, that's also a huge part of generating the economic driver for that segment. And we're seeing things like drones and ocean drones that are much cheaper than huge vessels that take up a lot of diesel. So we see things like that. In my own country, we are piloting a stablecoin for payment processing. Believe it or not, we have to air freight US dollars to Palau, and we have 350 islands. So you can imagine the logistics challenge of getting payments into a lot of these island countries. And we, we think by utilizing things like digital payments, that will also make societies more effective and more efficient and go a long way into promoting commerce within the islands. We're also piloting things like a digital registry similar to that countries can use to promote digital businesses. So I think some of those— these are emerging ideas, but they are kind of innovative in a way that SIDS can take advantage of them quickly. I think that's one of the things that we like to tell our partners. The size of SIDS as being small means that we can actually undertake projects very quickly. We can get resolutions and bills passed through our Congress in record speed. Which larger countries can't do. So I think so those are some of the competitive advantages that we see as SIDS, but we really are excited to launch into the implementation phase of ABASS and see what SIDS V will bring. Thank you.

Wonderful, thank you very, very much. I think that's a nice note for us all to end on there, that smallness is as much a source of nimbleness and innovation as it is of constraint. I'll hand back to the chair.

I would also like to thank the distinguished panelists and delegations for their substantive presentations and statements. We have thus completed our program of work for this meeting. The forum will reconvene tomorrow at 10 AM. To continue with its program of work. Detailed information on the program is available on the HLPF website. Thank you very much, one and all. Have a very pleasant evening. The meeting is adjourned.
